title: Spot the bug, then solve
idea: LOOP: reuse the debugging eye from Units 66-67 on mixed list code, then write the correct version. No new concept.

exercises.prompt:
This should sum [2, 3, 5] to 10:

total = 1
for n in [2, 3, 5]:
    total = total + n
print(total)

What prints, and why?
exercises.explanation: 1 + 2 + 3 + 5 = 11, one too high. The wrong start of 1 is the bug; it should be 0.

exercises.prompt:
This should count items over 4 in [5, 9]:

count = 0
for n in [5, 9]:
    count = 0
    if n > 4:
        count = count + 1
print(count)

What prints?
options: 1 — 'count = 0' inside the loop resets it every pass
exercises.explanation: The reset-inside bug: only the last pass survives, so count is 1 though both items match. Move the reset above the loop.
'50 or more' includes 50, so use >=. With > 50 the boundary value 50 is wrongly dropped.

exercises.prompt:
This should print all 3 items of nums = [1, 2, 3]:

for i in range(len(nums) - 1):
    print(nums[i])

What goes wrong?
options: it skips the last item — the '- 1' is an off-by-one bug
exercises.explanation: range(len-1) = range(2) = 0,1, so item 3 is skipped. Remove the '- 1' to visit every index.

exercises.prompt:
This finds the biggest of [-4, -2]:

best = 0
for n in [-4, -2]:
    if n > best:
        best = n
print(best)

What prints, and why wrong?
options: 0 — but 0 isn't in the list; start best at the first item
exercises.explanation: No negative beats 0, so best stays 0 (not a list value). Start best at the first item to fix it.

exercises.prompt: Now write it RIGHT: sum [2, 3, 5] correctly. Arrange the code.
exercises.explanation: Start at 0, add each item, print. Prints 10 — the correct sum.

exercises.prompt: Knowing the common bug families makes you faster at BOTH fixing and writing correct code the first time.
exercises.explanation: Yes — the families (wrong start, reset-inside, off-by-one, wrong test, empty case) are a checklist you apply as you write.

exercises.prompt: Before trusting any list loop, a quick self-check is to...
options: ask: right start? reset above the loop? right comparison? empty case handled?
exercises.explanation: Running the bug-family checklist in your head catches most mistakes before they ever print a wrong answer.

exercises.prompt: Write it RIGHT: count items over 4 in [5, 9]. The correct start and test are...
options: count = 0 above the loop, test n > 4 inside
exercises.explanation: Set count = 0 once above the loop and test n > 4 inside. That gives 2 — both items counted.

exercises.prompt: The takeaway tying Laps 3-4 to debugging:
options: the same tools, written carefully, with the bug checklist, solve problems correctly
exercises.explanation: Solving and debugging are two sides of one skill: apply the familiar tools and watch for the familiar bugs.
